allClaimsInDocs.claim_text: The claim 'vaccines do not cause autism' is not an evidence-based claim because studies have not ruled out the possibility that infant vaccines cause autism.
The CDC's revised guidance on vaccines and autism undermines scientific integrity and reverses the burden of proof.
The CDC's change in guidance about vaccines and autism raises concerns about scientific integrity.
The CDC claims that studies supporting a link between vaccines and autism have been ignored by health authorities.
The CDC's statement that vaccines do not cause autism is not evidence-based because studies have not ruled out the possibility that infant vaccines cause autism.
Science cannot prove universal negatives, and consistent, reproducible associations must be shown to establish links.
The fraudulent 1998 Lancet paper by Andrew Wakefield claimed a link between the MMR vaccine and autism.
Wakefield hid major financial conflicts of interest and failed to disclose payments from lawyers preparing a lawsuit against MMR manufacturers.
Wakefield committed serious ethical violations, including falsely claiming ethics approval for his study.
The fraudulent study by Wakefield continues to erode confidence in life-saving vaccines, leading to reduced vaccination rates and preventable illnesses.
Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. directed the CDC to change its vaccine guidance.

An investigation by journalist Brian Deer found that Wakefield, the author of the original research paper linking the vaccine to autism, had multiple undeclared conflicts of interest, had manipulated evidence, and had broken other ethical codes.
The scientific consensus is that there is no link between the MMR vaccine and autism.
The fraudulent research linking the MMR vaccine to autism has had significant public health repercussions.
The 1998 Lancet paper authored by Andrew Wakefield falsely claimed a link between the MMR vaccine and autism.
The Lancet paper was retracted in 2010, with its editor-in-chief describing it as 'utterly false'.
Promotion of the claimed link between MMR and autism has led to increased incidence of measles and mumps, resulting in deaths and serious injuries.
Multiple large epidemiological studies have found no link between the MMR vaccine and autism.
In 2011, a large-scale study conducted by Statens Serum Institut found no link between the MMR vaccine and autism.
A 2014 meta-analysis involving more than 1.25 million children found vaccinations are not associated with the development of autism.
The scientific consensus is that the vaccine's benefits greatly outweigh its potential risks.
The MMR vaccination compliance dropped sharply in the UK, from 92% in 1996 to 84% in 2002.
In 2008, measles was declared endemic in the UK for the first time in 14 years.
decades of high-quality, large-scale studies show that vaccines do not cause autism.
decades of high-quality, large-scale studies show that vaccines do not cause autism.
Vaccines are safe and do not cause autism or other chronic health conditions.
Vaccines undergo extensive testing and monitoring to ensure safety.
Vaccines are under constant study and must be tested in many steps before being added to the AAP Recommended Immunization Schedule.
The risk of a febrile seizure after getting the combined vaccine against measles, mumps, rubella and varicella (MMRV) is extremely low.

An analysis of 17 studies involving 10,935,541 vaccinated and 2,635,251 unvaccinated children concluded that COVID-19 vaccination was associated with lower risks of SARS-CoV-2 infection and hospitalization.
A 2021 report from the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality found no new evidence of increased risk of rare adverse events following routine childhood vaccinations.
A study found that vaccination did not increase the risk of children developing type 1 diabetes.
The AAP Recommended Child and Adolescent Immunization Schedule is based on expert review of all available evidence.
In 1998, a study claimed there was a link between the MMR vaccine and autism, but the results were later proven false and the study was retracted in 2010.
Former CDC leaders and current agency officials have said that career staff were not involved in or aware of the CDC update.
The CDC's revised claims about vaccines and autism are misleading and not supported by robust scientific evidence.
The CDC's revised webpage misrepresents the evidence regarding vaccines and autism.
The CDC's revised statement that 'vaccines do not cause autism' is 'not an evidence-based claim.'
The CDC webpage claims that studies supporting a link between vaccines and autism have been ignored by health authorities.
Numerous rigorous studies have repeatedly failed to identify any link between vaccination and autism.
Since 1998, independent researchers across seven countries have conducted more than 40 high-quality studies involving over 5.6 million people, concluding there’s no link between vaccines and autism.
The CDC webpage misinterprets stronger research that contradicts the idea that aluminum in vaccines is associated with autism.
Studies have repeatedly failed to find a link between MMR vaccines and autism.
A 2014 study by a researcher with ties to anti-vaccine groups claimed to have found a correlation between aluminum in vaccines and autism.
The CDC replaced its webpage on autism and vaccines on Nov. 19.
The childhood vaccination schedule has increased significantly since 1986.
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention website has been changed to promote false information suggesting vaccines cause autism.
The CDC's recent changes to vaccine safety statements may undermine public trust and fuel vaccine hesitancy.
The CDC's updated position on vaccines and autism raises concerns about public health and vaccine hesitancy.
The CDC's recent statement raises concerns about vaccine safety and autism links, igniting debate among health experts.
Health experts are raising the alarm, as decades of research confirm that there is no substantial link between vaccines and autism.
The CDC's abrupt reversal has created an information vacuum at a time when trust in public health is already strained.
A nationwide study in Denmark of 1.2 million children found no association between vaccines and aluminum in vaccines and confirmed that they are safe.
The misconception that vaccines lead to the development of autism dates to a study performed by Andrew Wakefield and 12 of his colleagues in 1998.
Wakefield et al were guilty of deliberate fraud—cherry-picking data that suited their case and falsifying facts.
The US is already confronting rising measles outbreaks, slipping vaccination rates, and increasing skepticism toward childhood immunizations.
The CDC updated its website and retracted a statement establishing that vaccines do not cause autism.
Since 1998, independent researchers across 7 countries have conducted more than 40 high-quality studies involving over 5.6 million people.
The polio vaccine has been a key component of childhood vaccine schedules, and as of 2025, polio can be considered a disease of the past.
